summary: Mark Ferrari surveys the history and craft of 8-bit and 8-bit-ish art, tracing the evolution from strict 16-color EGA palettes and early dithering at Lucasfilm Games to richer 256-color work and the later revival of the retro aesthetic in modern titles like Thimbleweed Park. He details techniques born from constraint—dithering, color cycling, and palette shifting—and demonstrates how artists could simulate movement, time of day, weather, and depth with careful palette management, rather than brute-frame animation. Ferrari contrasts historical tools (Deluxe Paint, D-Paint) with contemporary options (Promotion) and shares pragmatic studio workflows in Photoshop for achieving a retro look, including lighting templates, near-neighbor sampling, and anti-aliasing discipline. The talk interleaves technical demonstrations, live Q&A, and reflections on why the 8-bit look remains compelling despite modern resources, framing 8-bit-ish art as a creatively manageable space that still rewards deliberate color choice and clever structuring of limited palettes.
title: 8 Bit & '8 Bitish' Graphics—Outside the Box: Palette, Dither, and Color Cycling
